Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: This species is widespread throughout New Guinea. It is absent from the Trans-Fly in the island's south, where the predominant eucalyptus woodland does not provide suitable habitat (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). A record from Meruake reported by Rawlings and Donnellan (2003) was undoubtedly collected elsewhere, and extensive surveys in this area have never recorded the species (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). In Indonesian New Guinea it has been recorded on the offshore islands of Biak and Supiori, Yapen, Numfor and Num in Papua Province. In West Papua Province it has been recorded on the offshore islands of Batanta, Kofiau, Misool, Salawati and Waigeo and in Maluku Province it has been recorded on the Aru islands (McDowell 1975). In Australia it is restricted to the Iron and McIlwraith Ranges in the northeast Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, and adjacent areas. It is found at elevations from sea level to 2,000 m asl (McDowell 1975).
documentation.population: In Australia the species appears to occur in three isolated populations (Natusch and Natusch 2011).Subpopulations in New Guinea have been documented to be genetically deeply divergent due to the central cordillera that acts as a barrier for gene flow (Rawlings and Donnellan 2003, Natusch and Lyons 2014). Natusch and Natusch (2011) documented different age profiles and abundance estimates between two of their study sites with density estimates of 540 km–2 in the Iron Range and 200 km–2 in the McIlwraith Range, where the percentages of mature individuals captured were 56% and 83%, respectively. They suggest that this could be due to differences in prey abundance, or that collection for the pet trade in the Iron Range area has skewed the population demographic towards immature snakes. The latter interpretation is speculative, as the number of Morelia viridis individuals collected in this area is not known and it is not clear whether it is sufficient to alter population demographics. A wet season survey recorded an average of one individual per 20 minutes in the Iron Range (C. Hoskin pers. comm. 2017).
documentation.habitats: Morelia viridis is restricted to primarily to closed forest habitats, but will also utilize other habitats adjacent to closed forests (Natusch and Natusch 2011). The species has also been recorded in regrowth areas and rural gardens in New Guinea (O'Shea 1996). It is an arboreal species, however it descends to the ground to hunt at night (Wilson et al. 2006). It is a nocturnal, ‘sit and wait’ predator that feeds primarily on lizards (especially skinks) as a juvenile, before switching to feed primarily on small mammals as an adult (Natusch and Lyons 2014). Morelia viridis males reach sexual maturity at approximately 91 cm and females at 112 cm SVL (Natusch and Lyons 2014). It is an oviparous species with a clutch size of between 6-32 eggs and incubation period of around 52 days. Captive individuals have been observed to mate, deposit eggs and hatch throughout the year, however the reproductive cycle in wild individuals occurs during the winter (dry season months (July - November) (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). This species goes through ontogenetic changes in color and pattern. (Barker and Barker 1994, O’Shea 1996, Allison et al. 1998, Cermak 2008, Natusch and Natusch 2011, Natusch and Lyons 2012).
documentation.threats: This species is popular in the pet trade due to its attractive color. The natural color morphs and need for fresh bloodlines have resulted in the constant capture of wild specimens for the pet trade (Lyons and Natusch 2013). Despite being illegal, the collection of Morelia viridis is still occurring. Lyons and Natusch (2011) indicate that the harvest of M. viridis may be threatening some subpopulations, in particular those on isolated islands. This species has nevertheless been utilized for decades (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2010), and pressure on wild subpopulations may have decreased in recent years due to extensive captive breeding. In the past, collection may have impacted population demographics in the Iron Range (Natusch and Natusch 2011), but it remains common and the inaccessible McIlwraith subpopulation is thought to be secure (Natusch and Natusch 2011, C. Hoskin pers. comm. 2017). Of the highest concern is the subpopulation on Biak Island in Papua Province, Indonesian New Guinea (Lyons and Natusch 2011). Indigenous people in New Guinea also hunt this species for food, and while this is a longstanding traditional practice it may represent an additional pressure on subpopulations depleted through harvesting for trade.
documentation.measures:
Morelia viridis is listed under Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). This species has protected status in Australia, Papua New Guinea and Indonesia (Natusch and Lyons 2012) and occurs in numerous protected areas.

There is evidence that M. viridis exported from Indonesia as captive-bred are in fact wild-caught (Lyons and Natusch 2011). This trade has skewed the population demographics of some island subpopulations, which may be indicative of unsustainable levels of offtake. It appears that breeding M. viridis is currently not a cheap alternative to laundering wild-caught animals and is therefore not fulfilling the conservation objectives that led to the establishment of farms. Nevertheless, for most subpopulations harvesting is not considered a major threat, and laundering of specimens through farms is a compliance problem rather than a conservation issue (Natusch 2018). Because M. viridis is primarily restricted to closed forest habitats, protection of these habitats is the most important challenge for conserving this species. The expansion of oil palm plantations in West Papua and Papua, Indonesia, and subsequent habitat loss through increasing development in the region, is the most significant threat to the conservation of this species
documentation.use_trade:
This snake is among the more commonly traded reptiles in Indonesian New Guinea (Natusch and Lyons 2012). Natusch and Lyons (2012) found, in a study on the Indonesian reptile pet trade that eleven of fifteen (73%) traders indicated that some species (including, M. viridis) had become particularly scarce due, in part, to over-collection as well as habitat loss at historic collection sites. The large harvests of  M. viridis recorded, coupled with anecdotal evidence of species declines, suggest that the ongoing harvest and trade of this species for pets may be detrimental to wild subpopulations. Lyons and Natusch (2011) found that this trade had already impacted island populations of M. viridis (Natusch and Lyons 2012).

Natusch and Lyons (2012) reported numbers of individuals found in Aru (123 individuals), Biak (1,025 individuals), Jayapura (70 individuals), Merauke (29 individuals) and the Vogelkop (176 individuals) at wildlife traders between September 2010 – April 2011. This species is listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) and has protected status in Indonesia, however there is no export quota for this species and under CITES regulations no restriction on the number of farmed or captive-bred individuals that can be exported. Many Indonesian breeding farms illegally launder wild-caught green pythons and export them under the guise of being captive-bred (Natusch and Lyon 2011). In 1996-2012 the number of imports of captive-bred M. viridis increased by 1767% consisting of 0.4% of the total trade (Robinson et al. 2015).

Indigenous people in New Guinea also hunt this species for food.

The species is collected for the pet trade in Australia, likely taken mainly from the Iron Range population (C. Hoskin and P. Couper pers. comm. 2017). Prices online have decreased in recent years, apparently as a consequence of extensive captive breeding (C. Hoskin pers. comm. 2017).
documentation.rationale: Morelia viridis has been assessed as Least Concern. It has a widespread distribution through New Guinea its associated offshore islands and northeast Australia. It is abundant throughout the majority of its range, inhabits a wide range of closed forest habitats, and is not thought to be declining sufficiently rapidly across its range as a whole to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is present in many protected areas in New Guinea and Australia. Despite wild harvest being illegal it is one of the more commonly traded reptile species in Indonesian New Guinea. This may not be affecting the species as a whole but the harvest of M. viridis may threaten some localized populations and in particular, those on isolated islands. Of highest concern is the subpopulation on Biak Island in Papua Province, Indonesian New Guinea.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Molecular analysis conducted by Rawlings and Donnellan (2003) found that Morelia viridis consists of two monophyletic lineages, corresponding to a north-south division in the region of New Guinea's central cordillera. These authors discussed the possibility that these two clades warranted recognition as two distinct species based on the degree of sequence divergence. They were unable to reliably determine range limits due to limited sampling along the apparent contact zone and declined to take taxonomic action pending further analysis, including the more thorough use of nuclear genes with wider geographic sampling. Rawlings and Donnellan (2003) noted that McDowell (1975) did not identify any morphological characters in New Guinean green pythons that appear to correspond to these clades and reported that there was no clear geographic barrier between the two taxa.

The northern clade, which was not named by Rawlings and Donnellan (2003), was associated with the available name Chondropython azureus Meyer, 1874 by Schleip and O'Shea (2010). Barker et al. (2015) coined the combination Morelia azurea for this taxon and designated a neotype, recognizing this taxon as the sister species to M. viridis. As the further research recommended by Rawlings and Donnellan (2003) has not been conducted to confirm the status and distribution limits of M. azurea, it is here retained within M. viridis.
